The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and

2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then

3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with

hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and

between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, with vector-valued functions, their
components $f_i = \pi_i \circ f$, their limits and their continuity as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

1. **Continuity is componentwise.** Let $(X,d_X)$ be a metric space, $A \subseteq X$,
   $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $a \in A$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and
   only if every component $f_i : A \to \mathbb{R}$ $(i<m)$ is continuous at $a$.
2. **Limits are componentwise.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
   point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let
   $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. Then $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if
   $\lim_{x\to c} f_i(x) = L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[def-function-limit]]).
3. **Algebra.** Let $(X,d_X)$, $A$, $a$ be as in clause 1, let
   $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous at $a$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
   Then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ (defined pointwise) are continuous at $a$; the
   real-valued function $x \mapsto \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); and for every norm $N$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the real-valued function $x \mapsto N(f(x))$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

derivations.claim: The coordinate path $y$ is continuous at the corners and the endpoints of the piece by [L1] and $C^{1}$ on $(\alpha,\beta)$, so $y$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$; on $(\alpha,\beta)$ each coordinate derivative $y^{j'}$ is continuous by [L1], and by the chart form [L2] one has $-\eta(x'(u),x'(u)) = (y^{0'}(u))^{2} - |z'(u)|^{2}$ for every $u \in (\alpha,\beta)$.

At every $u \in (\alpha,\beta)$ the tangent $x'(u)$ is nonzero future causal, so by [L3] $y^{0'}(u) \ge |z'(u)| \ge 0$ and $y^{0'}(u) > 0$: the spatial inequality uses the coordinate description of the future cone, and strict positivity uses that $x'(u) \ne 0$ rules out the case $y'(u) = 0$.
For $\alpha < u < v < \beta$ and each $j \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ the truncated fundamental theorem gives $\int_u^v y^{j'} = y^{j}(v) - y^{j}(u)$ by [L4].

Letting $u \downarrow \alpha$ in the case $j = 0$ of step 2.2, continuity of $y^{0}$ at $\alpha$ gives $\lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} \int_u^r y^{0'} = y^{0}(r) - y^{0}(\alpha)$, a finite real number; it is nonnegative because $y^{0'}(\cdot) \ge 0$ on $(u,r)$ and [L5] applies to the truncations, $y^{0}(r) - y^{0}(\alpha) \ge 0$.
Likewise $\lim_{v \uparrow \beta} \int_r^v y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta) - y^{0}(r)$, finite and nonnegative.

The functions $|z'|$ and $f = \sqrt{(y^{0'})^{2}-|z'|^{2}}$ are continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ and satisfy $0 \le |z'| \le y^{0'}$ and $0 \le f \le y^{0'}$ there: $|z'|^{2}$ is a finite sum of squares of the continuous functions $z'^{i}$, hence continuous by [L8]; writing $t := |z'|^{2}$, the composite $t^{1/2}$ is continuous where $t > 0$ by [L8], and at a point where $t(u_0) = 0$ the estimate $0 \le |z'(u)| = (|z'(u)|^{2})^{1/2} \le (\sup_{|u-u_0| < \delta}|z'|^{2})^{1/2} < \varepsilon$ for small $\delta$, using monotonicity of the square root and continuity of $|z'|^{2}$ at $u_0$, gives continuity there; the same argument applies to $f$, whose inner function $(y^{0'})^{2}-|z'|^{2}$ is continuous and nonnegative by step 2.1; and the domination $f \le y^{0'}$, $|z'| \le y^{0'}$ follows from $0 \le (y^{0'})^{2} - |z'|^{2} \le (y^{0'})^{2}$, $y^{0'} \ge 0$ and monotonicity of the square root, together with $(y^{0'})^{2}$'s unique nonnegative square root $y^{0'}$ from [L8].

For each $j$, step 2.2 gives $\int_u^r y^{j'} = y^{j}(r)-y^{j}(u)$ and $\int_r^v y^{j'} = y^{j}(v)-y^{j}(r)$; letting $u \downarrow \alpha$ and $v \uparrow \beta$, continuity of $y^{j}$ at $\alpha$ and $\beta$ gives the finite limits $y^{j}(r)-y^{j}(\alpha)$ and $y^{j}(\beta)-y^{j}(r)$, whose sum is $y^{j}(\beta)-y^{j}(\alpha)$: the signed improper integral of each coordinate derivative equals the corresponding endpoint increment.

1. **Continuity is componentwise.** Let $(X,d_X)$ be a metric space, $A \subseteq X$,
   $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $a \in A$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and
   only if every component $f_i : A \to \mathbb{R}$ $(i<m)$ is continuous at $a$.
2. **Limits are componentwise.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
   point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let
   $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. Then $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if
   $\lim_{x\to c} f_i(x) = L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[def-function-limit]]).
3. **Algebra.** Let $(X,d_X)$, $A$, $a$ be as in clause 1, let
   $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous at $a$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
   Then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ (defined pointwise) are continuous at $a$; the
   real-valued function $x \mapsto \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); and for every norm $N$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the real-valued function $x \mapsto N(f(x))$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly

automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over

is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of

([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, with vector-valued functions, their
components $f_i = \pi_i \circ f$, their limits and their continuity as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

1. **Continuity is componentwise.** Let $(X,d_X)$ be a metric space, $A \subseteq X$,
   $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and $a \in A$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and
   only if every component $f_i : A \to \mathbb{R}$ $(i<m)$ is continuous at $a$.
2. **Limits are componentwise.** Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit
   point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let
   $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. Then $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ if and only if
   $\lim_{x\to c} f_i(x) = L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[def-function-limit]]).
3. **Algebra.** Let $(X,d_X)$, $A$, $a$ be as in clause 1, let
   $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous at $a$ and let $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
   Then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ (defined pointwise) are continuous at $a$; the
   real-valued function $x \mapsto \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); and for every norm $N$ on
   $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the real-valued function $x \mapsto N(f(x))$ is continuous at
   $a$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a

Both $x$ and $y$ are weak piecewise future timelike curves (the first by hypothesis, the second by steps 3.1 and 4.1), so the improper integrals of $f$ over the pieces of $x$ and of $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}$ over the pieces of $y$ exist and are finite by [L9]. vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and

coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$

frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when

families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all

first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

$c^{-1}\sqrt{g_x}$, evaluated at $b$ on $[a,b]$
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations with everywhere
positive derivative is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

by oriented additivity ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]); equivalently,
the increment is the integral function with base point $a$ of the density
$c^{-1}\sqrt{g_x}$, evaluated at $b$ on $[a,b]$
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations with everywhere
positive derivative is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts

and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$

basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.
